body.x: Security guards on night and holiday shifts, large grounds with blind spots between fixed cameras, and buildings where a patrol has to climb stairs from floor to floor are all places where coverage gaps tend to open up. People alone find it hard to close them.

DOGU Robotics, a Daegu company that builds AI-powered autonomous patrol robots, says it has designed its business around those gaps. Founded in 2017 by CEO Jinhyo Kim, who studied autonomous robot technology in graduate school, the company is returning to FIX after showing its indoor patrol robot iroi at FIX 2024. This year it will exhibit at the 15th Daegu International Robot Industry Expo (ROBEX 2026), which its application describes as the robotics sector of FIX 2026.

According to DOGU, Kim's work is to have robots take over repetitive and hazardous patrols so that people can concentrate on judgment and response. The company develops its patrol robots and the software that runs them in-house. Its full-stack solution includes SOS (Security Operation System), which runs and manages multiple robots from one place, and Planner, AI-based robot control software. DOGU says that when a robot detects an abnormal situation in the video it captures on patrol, operators can check the site in real time and respond, and that its 3D navigation technology gives robots the floor-to-floor connection data they need to patrol multistory buildings. In the company's words, the system supports on-site staff rather than replacing them, because robots flag events and people decide.

The lineup includes iroi, an indoor patrol robot with a 21-inch touch display and an ultraviolet (UV) sterilization lamp for guidance and disinfection in spaces without GPS; Patrover, an outdoor robot for night patrols and video-based anomaly detection; and Robjet, a multipurpose modular robot configured for each site. A quadruped patrol solution developed with Rainbow Robotics extends coverage to stairs and rough terrain. DOGU manages development, production and field operations under ISO 9001, 14001 and 45001 certified systems and holds Korea's outdoor mobile robot operational safety certification.

At ROBEX 2026, the company will present what it calls Physical AI field solutions that carry the autonomous driving and monitoring technology from its patrol operations over to humanoid and quadruped robots. The first is a humanoid demonstration of R-noid, which Robot.com commercially launched at Automate 2026 in June. DOGU says R-noid combines a humanoid upper body with a wheeled base for stability, with dual 7-degree-of-freedom arms and a torso reaching nearly two meters, so it can work at shelves and workstations designed for people. It targets repetitive, hard-to-staff tasks such as packing, picking and customer guidance, and Robot.com offers it as a Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS) solution that can go from the first site visit to autonomous operation in as little as eight to 12 weeks. DOGU will demonstrate three humanoid models, including R-noid, in work scenarios designed for deployment in Korea.

The second is the quadruped AI patrol solution, which combines a quadruped robot platform with DOGU's AI patrol payload and monitoring software for video-based anomaly detection and remote monitoring across large, complex industrial sites such as plants, logistics centers and underground facilities. The third is SOS integrated monitoring, which shows the location, status and alerts of multiple robots on one screen. DOGU says it is extending its autonomy, AI perception and monitoring technology beyond any single robot so it can propose the right mix of iroi, Patrover, Robjet, quadruped robots and partner humanoids for each site, and that experience from more than 100 sites in Korea carries over to each new platform.

DOGU gives three reasons for exhibiting. It wants to show how AI technology refined through patrol operations since 2017 is expanding to humanoid and quadruped robots, which it says fits the FIX 2026 theme of AI moving beyond technology into everyday life. It wants to introduce a Korea-U.S. robotics collaboration model, in which it brings humanoids from Robot.com, which the company says operates more than 500 robots across the U.S., Canada and the Middle East, to sites in Korea. And through the pre-matched export consultations and domestic purchase consultations at FIX 2026, it plans to meet domestic customers and overseas buyers, hold adoption talks with live demonstrations, and strengthen ties with the Daegu robotics ecosystem.

In Korea, the company says it has supplied patrol robot solutions to public institutions, major corporations and security service providers including the Korean National Police Agency, POSCO, LG Electronics, KT, S-1 and SK shieldus, and has secured more than 100 sites nationwide across local governments, military facilities, industrial sites, general hospitals and universities. iroi handles patrol, guidance and disinfection at large hospitals, public institutions, shopping malls, smart farms and exhibition centers, and has supported security at university campuses such as Chonnam National University. In July 2026, it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Jihyo Elementary School in Goyang, Gyeonggi Province, to deploy Patrover for night campus patrols. In March 2026, it was invited to show its robots at Port Week of the Clipper Round the World Yacht Race in Tongyeong. It also worked with Dongguk University on a semi-humanoid iroi prototype with robotic arms, which was trialed as a temple guide at Bongeunsa Temple in Seoul, and it signed an agreement with Rainbow Robotics in 2025 for the quadruped solution.

The U.S. is its export market. DOGU says it prepared by joining the K-Startup Center (KSC) in Seattle in 2024 and set up a U.S. subsidiary, DOGU, Inc., the same year. After exhibiting at ISC West in 2025 it began winning local customers, and it now runs sales and technical support from Silicon Valley (San Jose). The company reports that iroi is deployed at SK hynix America and that it has signed a long-term service contract with Dolby for its Sunnyvale site, with expansion to Dolby's San Francisco headquarters under way. In July 2026, DOGU signed an MOU with San Francisco-based robotics platform company Robot.com and exported about USD 2 million of products including iroi, and the two are pursuing joint sales, marketing, channel development and exhibitions in North America. DOGU says its U.S. work bundles SOS with local installation and maintenance, with field engineers at the U.S. subsidiary handling site mapping, patrol route design and on-site response while the research team in Korea provides remote support. It has no exports outside the U.S. but has set up a Southeast Asia base in Singapore hosted at Infineon Technologies and exhibited at COMPUTEX 2026 in June as a partner of Taiwan's YUAN High-Tech. It also showed iroi at CES 2024, the modular Robjet S5 at CES 2025, and returned to ISC West in 2026.

Its priority markets are the U.S., Southeast Asia centered on Singapore, and Taiwan, chosen for the cost of people-based security, the policy environment for robot adoption and whether DOGU already has a local partner or base. For the U.S., the company points to guard turnover and rising labor costs and to growing interest in Korean-built patrol robots with in-house monitoring software, and it plans to extend to corporate campuses, universities, residential communities and logistics and manufacturing facilities. In Singapore, it plans to build operating cases with local security service companies before moving to neighboring countries. In Taiwan, it received inquiries from local security companies after COMPUTEX 2026 and wants to turn them into deployments.

The company lists five difficulties. Local certification and compliance take time and money, since U.S. supply requires Federal Communications Commission (FCC) certification for wireless equipment and electrical and safety certifications such as UL, which must be reviewed again whenever parts change. Evaluations are long, as global companies, universities and public institutions review security, IT networks, data governance and insurance, and DOGU says initial deployment has taken about five to nine months. Technical localization means adapting to conditions such as offices with much glass and mirrors, large-site wireless networks and U.S. license plates. Logistics, customs and local operating infrastructure add costs, as does finding local partners and building brand awareness as a new brand in the U.S. DOGU says continued support for certification costs, overseas regulatory information, local demonstration opportunities and overseas exhibitions and logistics would help Korean robotics companies establish themselves abroad faster.

Its plan rests on three pillars: expanding U.S. references, extending to more robot platforms and building a base in Southeast Asia. In the U.S., DOGU intends to add sites at existing customers, diversify through joint sales with Robot.com, extend into outdoor patrol and parking lot security, and obtain FCC and UL certifications in stages. It will keep upgrading iroi, Patrover and Robjet, including a new Patrover model, while running its AI patrol payload and monitoring software on quadruped robots, humanoids and other platforms. It is reviewing a local entity in Singapore and will pursue deployment of humanoids in Korea through Robot.com. Domestically, it aims to turn meetings with overseas buyers at exhibitions such as FIX 2026 into exports, and to grow beyond a patrol robot company into a Physical AI company.

DOGU names its main customers as facility and safety managers at public institutions and local governments, police patrol departments, large general hospitals, steel, chemical and semiconductor plants, university and school safety offices, and unmanned security service companies in Korea. In the U.S. they are the facilities and security teams at tech and semiconductor campuses, university public safety departments, multifamily property managers and logistics and manufacturing security chiefs, and in Singapore, the operations heads of security service companies.

Now in its third year, FIX 2026 (Future Innovation Technology Expo) is a future-industry exhibition that brings together and connects innovative technologies in future mobility, robotics, AI and ICT, and startups. It runs from Wednesday, Oct. 21, to Saturday, Oct. 24, at EXCO in Daegu. Under the theme "AI, Beyond Tech into Reality," the exhibition shares industry trends and core technologies through AI-based technology exhibitions, conferences and lectures by experts from Korea and abroad, and networking programs.
